headline: 5 lessons from Atomic Habits
intro_line: James Clear's Atomic Habits sold millions of copies for one reason: it makes change feel small enough to actually do.

lessons.detail: Goals set direction, but you fall to the level of your systems. Design the routine, not just the target.
Tiny gains feel invisible day to day, but 1% better every day is roughly 37x better over a year.
Most habits fail on friction, not willpower. Put the running shoes by the door; delete the app from the home screen.

lessons.lesson: Change your identity, not just your behavior
lessons.detail: Don't aim to 'run a marathon.' Aim to 'become a runner.' Every action is a vote for the person you're becoming.
One missed day is an accident. Two is the start of a new pattern. The rule that protects a habit is bouncing back fast.

closing_line: You don't need a bigger goal. You need a smaller, more obvious first step you can repeat tomorrow.

headline: 7 lessons from The Psychology of Money
intro_line: Morgan Housel's central claim: doing well with money has little to do with how smart you are, and everything to do with how you behave.

lessons.lesson: Wealth is what you don't see
lessons.detail: Real wealth is income not spent. The visible stuff — cars, watches — is money leaving, not money kept.
The hardest financial skill is stopping the goalposts from moving. Knowing when you have enough beats always wanting more.

lessons.lesson: Room for error is the point
lessons.detail: Plans fail. The people who survive leave margin — savings, slack, low fixed costs — so a bad year doesn't end the game.
Compounding rewards patience over brilliance. The longest runway usually beats the highest return.
Not every outcome is earned. Judge decisions by the process, not just the result.
You don't need a specific goal to save. Savings buys options and control over your time — which is the highest dividend money pays.
People's money choices make sense given their own history and fears. Understanding that makes you calmer with your own.

closing_line: The goal isn't to be the smartest person with money. It's to be reasonable, patient, and hard to knock out of the game.
